title: How does Kafka guarantee message ordering within a partition, and what happens with multiple consumers (one consumer per partition per group)?
shortTitle: How Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition, and multiple consumers

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka guarantees ordering by making each partition a strictly ordered, append-only log where every record receives a sequential offset. A producer appends records to a partition in the order it sends them, and a consumer reads them back in exactly that offset order. Ordering is guaranteed only within a single partition, never across partitions. Within a consumer group, Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer, so no two consumers in the same group ever read the same partition concurrently, which is what preserves the single-reader, in-order guarantee.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine one drawer of the National Bank of India ledger where pages are glued in sequence — page 0, page 1, page 2 — and nobody can shuffle them. Only one clerk is ever allowed to read that drawer for a given team, so he reads page 0, then page 1, then page 2, exactly in order. If the bank added a second clerk to the same team, Kafka would not let both read the same drawer; it hands each clerk a different drawer so there is never a race over the same pages.
s1_definition.oneliner: Order is guaranteed per partition because records get sequential offsets and exactly one consumer per group reads each partition.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka guarantees ordering by making each partition a strictly ordered, append-only log where every record receives a sequential offset. A producer appends records to a partition in the order it sends them, and a consumer reads them back in exactly that offset order. Ordering is guaranteed only within a single partition, never across partitions. Within a consumer group, Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer, so no two consumers in the same group ever read the same partition concurrently, which is what preserves the single-reader, in-order guarantee.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine one drawer of the National Bank of India ledger where pages are glued in sequence — page 0, page 1, page 2 — and nobody can shuffle them. Only one clerk is ever allowed to read that drawer for a given team, so he reads page 0, then page 1, then page 2, exactly in order. If the bank added a second clerk to the same team, Kafka would not let both read the same drawer; it hands each clerk a different drawer so there is never a race over the same pages.

**One line to remember:** Order is guaranteed per partition because records get sequential offsets and exactly one consumer per group reads each partition.

sections.s2_technical:
Ordering starts at the producer. When a producer sends records to a partition, Kafka appends them in send order and assigns each one the next offset. The partition is immutable, so once a record sits at offset 5, nothing can insert a record before it. A consumer always reads a partition sequentially from a starting offset forward, so it observes records in the same order the producer wrote them.

The partition a record lands in is decided by its key. If you produce with a key, Kafka hashes the key to choose a partition, so all records with the same key go to the same partition and are therefore ordered relative to one another. In banking, keying by account id with `kafkaTemplate.send("transactions", "SAV2001", event)` guarantees Rajesh's debit, balance check, and next debit are read in the exact order they occurred. Records with different keys may go to different partitions, where Kafka makes no cross-partition ordering promise.

There is a producer subtlety. With retries enabled and more than one in-flight request per connection, a failed-then-retried batch could theoretically be reordered. To prevent this you enable idempotence with `enable.idempotence=true`, which Kafka sets by default in modern versions, and it keeps `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` at five or fewer while preserving order. This ensures ordering holds even across retries.

Now the multiple-consumers part. A consumer group is a set of consumers sharing a group id. Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer in that group; it never splits a partition between two consumers of the same group. So if a topic has three partitions and the group has three consumers, each consumer owns one partition and processes it in order. If the group has two consumers, one consumer owns two partitions and the other owns one. If the group has four consumers but the topic has only three partitions, the fourth consumer sits idle because there is no partition left to assign. This one-consumer-per-partition rule is precisely what preserves ordering under parallelism.

Across different consumer groups the story changes: each group gets its own independent assignment of all partitions, so the fraud group and the audit group both read every partition, each in order, without affecting each other. Ordering is still per partition within each group.

The senior-level nuance is that you trade global ordering for throughput, and you manage this with the key. If a use case truly needs total ordering you must use a single partition, which caps throughput to one consumer. Most banking use cases only need per-entity ordering, so keying by account id gives both order where it matters and parallelism everywhere else. Another nuance is that increasing partitions later changes the key-to-partition mapping, so a key that was ordered in one partition could split across two after a repartition, which is why partition count is planned up front.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India had a bug where a customer's balance check sometimes ran before the debit that preceded it, giving a wrong balance, and the team must fix ordering while still scaling consumers.

Problem 1 — Rajesh does a debit of 50000 and immediately checks his balance. If these two events are processed out of order, the balance check reports the old, higher balance, confusing the customer. This is exactly the per-partition ordering problem — both events must be keyed by the same account id so they share one partition and are read in order.

Problem 2 — The team wants to run several consumer instances to handle peak load, but they fear two instances might process the same account's events at the same time and still reorder them. This is exactly the one-consumer-per-partition-per-group rule — Kafka guarantees only one consumer in the group reads a given partition, so there is no race.

Problem 3 — The fraud team also needs every event, but must not slow down the main processor. This is exactly the separate-consumer-group behavior — a different group reads all partitions independently.

The mini-project simulates this. We build an `AccountEvent` domain object, an `OrderedPartition` that assigns sequential offsets, a `Topic` that routes by account id, and a `GroupAssignment` that enforces exactly one consumer per partition. The demo shows Rajesh's events kept in order on one partition, two consumers each owning distinct partitions, and a second group reading everything independently.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four events: E1 (debit), E2 (balance check), E3 (debit) for SAV2001, and E4 (credit) for CUR3001.

Step 1 — The topic is created with 3 partitions, each an empty ordered log.

Step 2 — E1 for SAV2001 is produced. The topic hashes SAV2001 to a partition, say partition 2, and appends E1 at offset 0.

Step 3 — E2 for SAV2001 hashes to the same partition 2 and is appended at offset 1, right after E1. The debit now precedes the balance check in the log, which is the whole point.

Step 4 — E3 for SAV2001 goes to partition 2 at offset 2. E4 for CUR3001 hashes to a different partition. Rajesh's three events are now strictly ordered in partition 2.

Step 5 — The main group has 2 consumers and 3 partitions. Kafka assigns partition 2 to exactly one consumer, so that consumer reads E1, E2, E3 in offset order. No other consumer in the group touches partition 2, so there is no race and no reordering.

Step 6 — The fraud group is a separate group with its own assignment. It reads all partitions independently, again in per-partition order, without slowing the main group. The balance bug is gone because the debit is always read before the balance check.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka guarantees message ordering within a partition because each partition is a strictly ordered, append-only log. When a producer sends records to a partition, Kafka appends them in send order and assigns each a sequential offset, and the partition is immutable, so nothing can be inserted before an existing record. A consumer reads the partition sequentially from a starting offset, so it sees records in exactly the order they were written. This ordering is guaranteed only within a single partition, never across partitions.

The partition a record lands in is chosen by its key. By keying events, I control what stays ordered. In my banking platform at National Bank of India, I key every transaction by account id, so Rajesh's debit, his balance check, and his next debit all land in the same partition and are read in the exact order they happened. That is what fixed a real bug we had where a balance check sometimes ran before the debit that preceded it.

The multiple-consumers part is governed by one rule: within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer. Kafka never lets two consumers in the same group read the same partition at the same time, which is precisely what preserves ordering under parallelism. If there are more consumers than partitions, the extra consumers sit idle. Across different consumer groups, each group gets its own full assignment, so the fraud group and the main processing group both read every partition independently, each in order, without interfering.

The senior nuance I always mention is that you trade global ordering for throughput, and the key is your lever. True total ordering requires a single partition, which caps you to one consumer. Most banking needs are only per-account ordering, so keying by account id gives order where it matters and parallelism everywhere else. I also enable producer idempotence so that retries never reorder records, which keeps the guarantee intact even when the network misbehaves.
